notes.meaning: Jewish captives sat down in deep sorrow along the canals and rivers of Babylon. Sitting on the ground was a common sign of mourning in the ancient world. Remembering Zion and its ruined temple brought them to tears. Even in a fertile foreign country, they could not forget their spiritual home.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Early church writer Augustine saw the waters of Babylon as a symbol of worldly, passing pleasures that Christians should weep beside rather than plunge into.

notes.meaning: The exiles put away their harps by hanging them on the poplar or willow trees along the riverbanks. Temple musicians had carried these instruments into captivity, hoping to play them again. Their overwhelming sadness silenced them, leaving the instruments untouched.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Augustine treated the harps as symbols of Scripture and God's promises, hung up away from unfruitful people who care only for worldly pleasures.

notes.meaning: The Babylonian conquerors demanded that their captives perform joyful songs for entertainment. They specifically asked to hear the sacred temple songs of Zion. To the crushed prisoners, turning holy worship songs into a spectacle for pagan masters felt cruel and humiliating.

other.label: Orthodox
other.view: Orthodox writers describe this demand as the crowning humiliation, treating sacred songs of praise like common tavern entertainment.

notes.meaning: The prisoners answered by asking how they could ever sing the Lord's holy songs in a land ruled by idolaters. These songs were sacred worship meant for God's presence, not amusement for captors. Deep grief made joyous celebration impossible while separated from the Promised Land.

The speaker vows never to forget Jerusalem, the place where God chose to dwell with His people. He calls a curse upon himself, wishing that his right hand would lose its skill to play the harp if he ever moved on from her memory. Loyalty to God meant keeping Jerusalem in his heart at all times.

The singer further vows that his tongue should stick to the roof of his mouth, making him unable to speak or sing, if he fails to remember Jerusalem. He resolves to value the restored worship of God far higher than any earthly pleasure. God's people find their deepest gladness in the health and honor of His kingdom.

other.label: Orthodox
other.view: Orthodox reflection teaches that believers living as strangers in the world must cherish the heavenly Jerusalem above every earthly joy.

notes.meaning: The psalmist calls on the Lord to remember and judge the Edomites for their betrayal. Though they were relatives descended from Esau, they cheered when Babylon tore down the walls of Jerusalem to the ground. Believers bring their pain over injustice directly to God, trusting Him to settle accounts.

The psalm speaks directly to the city and empire of Babylon, declaring that its ruin is already decided by God. Anyone who carries out God's judgment against Babylon will be performing a righteous act of justice. The cruelty Babylon dealt out to other nations will come right back upon its own head.

In ancient warfare, conquerors wiped out enemy populations completely, and Babylon had slaughtered Israel's infants in this exact way. This harsh verse declares that Babylon will receive the very destruction it brought on others, fulfilling God's announced judgment through future conquerors. It shows the awful end of an empire that showed no mercy.

differ.view: Many in the Reformed tradition view this prayer not as personal revenge, but as a holy desire for God's covenant justice to triumph fully over evil oppressors.

Some evangelicals believe Christians should not utter curses on human enemies, seeing these words as reflecting the brutal realities of ancient warfare rather than Christ's call to pursue reconciliation.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Augustine interpreted Babylon's infants allegorically as new sinful desires that Christians should immediately dash against Christ, the Rock, before they turn into sinful habits.
